connector: The girls have left Copenhagen for Uncle Henrik’s house by the sea. There is a meadow, a kitten, and the water, with Sweden a gray line on the far side. It feels safe. As you read, ask whether the danger has really gone away, and watch what Annemarie does with the secret she is keeping for Ellen.

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Grete. The city is behind you now. In this chapter you’ll smell the sea, walk through a meadow, and stand at the edge of the water looking at another country. But even here, there’s a secret to keep. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 7, and study one sentence closely. Today’s question: why can a small object carry so much weight?
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is about sorting. As you read, keep two lists in your head: what Annemarie feels, and what she does. The feelings tell you she’s human. The doing is your evidence. Watch especially for a quiet promise, and whether she keeps it.
transcripts.dol: The model is one calm sentence about a house. The sentence to fix has two sentences joined with no stop between them, and some names that need capitals: two girls and one country. Use the model to help you.
transcripts.guide1: Now the word work asks you to use what you’ve figured out. Study each model first. In grammar, you’ll pick the verb that matches its person-word. In spelling, you’ll join parts into one word, and some letters will try to trick you. Go slowly on the last line.
transcripts.morphology: Halfway across the water already. Two believing words, two stretching words. One of the stretching words is about acting as if something is true when it isn’t, which comes in handy in this story. Read each meaning, then choose the root that finishes the word.
transcripts.vocabulary: Match the words again. This time, try saying each meaning out loud in your own words before you tap. If you can explain a word to someone else, it belongs to you. Listen for these words as you read, too. Sometimes a writer never uses the word, but you can feel it on the page.
transcripts.grammar: Getting the verb to match its person-word isn’t about being fussy. When they don’t match, a reader trips. Read each sentence in a whisper and trust your ear. Then fix the last sentence, which has two mistakes, and say which word made you choose each fix.
transcripts.spelling: Adding parts to a word is like hooking cars onto a train. Each new car has to hook on properly. Sometimes a letter doubles, and sometimes a tricky spelling in the middle stays exactly as it was. Join each word carefully, then fix the line that went off the tracks.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about keeping something safe for someone else. When I was young, a neighbor gave me a small box to keep, and asked me to tell no one. I never opened it, and I never told. It felt like the most grown-up thing I had ever done. Watch what Annemarie promises Ellen in this chapter.
transcripts.read: Enjoy the beginning of this chapter. It’s the most peaceful place in the whole book so far: a meadow, a kitten, the sea. Then notice Mama’s questions when the girls come back from the shore. And pay attention at bedtime, when Ellen asks about something she’s missing.
transcripts.rwm: This sentence does three jobs at once. First you hear exactly what Annemarie says. Then you learn who said it. Then you learn when. Notice how that little tail at the end keeps the words tied to the story. In your own writing, a quote needs a tail like that too.
transcripts.guide3: Time to write. The questions ask about the necklace, what it means to Ellen, and why Sweden matters so much. Then you’ll write the first body paragraph of your essay. It has a reason, a piece of evidence from the book, and a sentence that ties them back to your claim.
transcripts.chapter: The last question asks why Sweden is important. You don’t need to know anything that hasn’t happened yet. Look at what the girls can see from the shore, and remember what you learned about Sweden earlier in this unit. Then explain what a free country so close by might mean.
transcripts.workshop: A body paragraph works like a sandwich with a purpose. Your reason goes on top. Your evidence from the book goes in the middle. And the last sentence connects it all back to what you believe. You only need one strong paragraph, so choose your best reason.

a.raw: ellen and annemarie walked to the meadow they could see sweden across the water
a.fixed: Ellen and Annemarie walked to the meadow. They could see Sweden across the water.
a.why: Capitals on Ellen, Annemarie and Sweden, a period after meadow, a capital T to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: annemarie showed ellen the sea it was too cold for swimming
b.fixed: Annemarie showed Ellen the sea. It was too cold for swimming.
b.why: Capitals on Annemarie and Ellen, a period after sea, a capital I to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why she hides it instead of throwing it away.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain why Ellen still wants it back someday.
scholar.journal-q3: … and explain how a free country so close by might change the way the characters feel.

g4w17cf1.h1: She is one person. A verb ending in y changes its y before it takes its ending.
g4w17cf1.why: carries: she is singular, so the verb takes an ending, and carry changes y to i first.

g4w17cf2.h1: They means more than one person. Does a plural pronoun add an ending to its verb?
g4w17cf2.why: hide: plural pronouns take the plain form of the verb.

g4w17cf3.h1: He is one person. What ending does a singular pronoun’s verb take?
g4w17cf3.why: asks: he is singular, so the verb ends in s.

g4w17cf4.h1: We means more than one, and the sentence is about the past. Which past form of be goes with we?
g4w17cf4.why: were: we, you and they take were; I, he, she and it take was.

s4w17cf1.h1: Keep the e in hope. The first suffix has only one l.
s4w17cf1.why: hopefully: hope + ful + ly. The two l’s meet only when ly is added.

s4w17cf2.h1: Nothing drops out here. Join all three parts exactly as they are.
s4w17cf2.why: carelessness: care + less + ness. Every letter stays.

s4w17cf3.h1: Watch the middle of friend: i comes before e.
s4w17cf3.why: unfriendly: un + friend + ly. The parts don’t change the base.

s4w17cf4.h1: The ending sounds like it could be spelled two ways. Here it uses an a.

match.intend: Intend has the root that means stretch. Look for the meaning about planning to do something on purpose.
match.credible: Credible has the root that means believe. Look for the meaning about being easy to believe.
match.discreet: Discreet is about being careful and quiet. Look for the meaning about not drawing attention.
match.tense: Tense is a feeling in your body. Look for the meaning about being tight with worry.

wordgame.voice: Tap a root, then the word it finishes. Or drag the root onto the word. Each stretching word reaches the light across the water; each believing word lights a window on the far shore.

why.t: In Chapter 7, Annemarie stands on the shore at Gilleleje and points across the sea to Sweden. tend means to stretch, so each right tend word stretches the lighthouse beam a little farther across the water. cred means to believe, so each right cred word lights a window on the far shore. One stretch of water each lesson, until the light reaches Sweden.

miss.fill1: Not quite. tend means stretch. Is incredible about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill2: Not quite. tend means stretch. Is credence about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill3: Not quite. cred means believe. Is pretend about believing, or about stretching?
miss.fill4: Not quite. cred means believe. Is attend about believing, or about stretching?

wordgame.winDay: The beam is almost there, and six windows glow across the water. One more lesson and the light will reach Sweden.
wordgame.win: The light reaches all the way across the water, and on the far shore, Kullen’s lighthouse answers. cred = believe, tend = stretch.

notes.wgrd: Feeling brave and acting brave are different. Sort what a character feels from what she does. Your evidence comes from the doing, even when it is quiet, like keeping a promise.
vocab: To plan to do something on purpose.
notes.wordParts: cred means “to believe” (credible, incredible). tend means “to stretch” or “to reach” (extend, pretend, attend).
notes.grammar: A pronoun and its verb must agree. With he, she or it, the verb takes an s: she watches, he listens. With I, you, we or they, it doesn’t: they wait.
notes.spelling: Many long words are built from parts: a prefix in front (un-, re-, dis-), a base word, and a suffix at the end (-ful, -ly, -ness, -ance). Find the base underneath and keep its spelling: hope + ful + ly = hopefully.

case.title: A Passport Stamped in Sweden
case.alt: An old, worn passport lying open, with stamps, handwriting and a large stamped word across one page.
label: This is a real passport. Its owner had been living in Denmark. In 1943 they were smuggled across the water to Sweden, and this passport was used to register them when they arrived.

In Chapter 7, Annemarie points across the sea and shows Ellen where Sweden is. Sweden was not at war, and German soldiers did not rule there. At its narrowest point, the water between Denmark and Sweden is less than three miles wide.

look.q: What do the stamps and writing in a passport show?
look.a: Who a person is, and where they have been allowed to go. Officials stamp a passport when someone arrives in a new country.

look.q: Why might a short stretch of water matter so much in 1943?
look.a: On one side, German soldiers were in charge. On the other side, they were not. Crossing it could mean being safe.

case.credit: A prewar Polish passport used to register in Sweden in 1943, after its owner was smuggled out of occupied Denmark. Photo: Huddyhuddy, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
case.sub: A real object from the war years.
